\chapter{Synthesis --- The Choices English Never Makes You Make}
\label{ch:spanish-synthesis-verb-splits}
\hlchaptermodality{77}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can choose correctly between three verb pairs where English offers only one word.}

preguntar/pedir, traer/llevar, conocer/saber - the decision carries the meaning.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Synthesis — the choices English never makes you make}

\label{lesson:ES-C39-sintesis-elegir}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new here. Two verbs to say aloud first: \emph{traer}, \emph{conocer}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one English word, two Spanish verbs}]
Three times now you have met a pair of verbs where English makes do with one. They arrived chapters apart and have never been put side by side:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{English gives you} & \textbf{Spanish makes you choose} & \textbf{the question you must answer} \\
\midrule
\textbf{to ask} & \emph{preguntar} · \emph{pedir} & asking a \textbf{question}, or asking \textbf{for a thing}? \\
\textbf{to bring / take} & \emph{traer} · \emph{llevar} & toward the speaker, or away? \\
\textbf{to know} & \emph{conocer} · \emph{saber} & a \textbf{person or place}, or a \textbf{fact}? \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

None of these is a vocabulary problem. In each one, the word is easy and the \textbf{decision} is the work — and the decision is information English speakers are simply never required to supply.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
When you pick \emph{traer} over \emph{llevar}, you have told your listener \textbf{where you are standing}. When you pick \emph{conocer} over \emph{saber}, you have told them whether you have \emph{met} the thing or only heard of it. The grammar is carrying meaning that English would need a whole clause to add.

You are not translating any more. You are choosing.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\begin{quote}
— ¿\textbf{Conoces} Madrid? — Sí, \textbf{conozco} Madrid. Pero no \textbf{sé} dónde está el café.
\end{quote}

Two \textquotedblleft{}knows\textquotedblright{} in two lines, and not interchangeable. The first is acquaintance — \emph{I have been there}. The second is a fact. English uses \textbf{know} for both and loses the difference.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the exchange above, both parts
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Until the choice happens before you notice making it.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does choosing \emph{traer} tell your listener? (\textbf{Where you are standing.}) What does choosing \emph{conocer} tell them? (That you have \textbf{met} it, not just heard of it.) And which of the three pairs did you learn first? (\emph{Preguntar} and \emph{pedir} — long before the other two.)
\end{tcolorbox}
